title: Social Media and Health: A Scoping Review of Behavioral and Health Outcomes
content: Background: Social media platforms have influenced health behaviors and outcomes, offering opportunities for health promotion while also posing risks such as promoting unhealthy habits and adverse mental health effects. This scoping review synthesizes the evidence on the multifaceted relationship between social media use and health, highlighting both positive and negative impacts to inform targeted interventions. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PubMed (MEDLINE), Cochrane Library, and ProQuest for studies published between January 2013 and January 2023. Search terms combined MeSH terms and keywords related to social media, health behaviors, and health outcomes. After screening 2,484 records, 26 studies were included. Data extraction focused on study characteristics, social media platforms, and impacts on behaviors and outcomes. Results: Included studies predominantly involved adolescents and young adults in the USA (n=14). Facebook was the most cited platform (88% of studies). Social media negatively influenced dietary habits, alcohol and tobacco use, physical activity, sleep, and risky sexual behaviors in most cases, but showed positive effects on COVID-19 preventive behaviors and cancer risk reduction. For outcomes, associations with body dissatisfaction and mental health issues were largely negative, though some studies reported protective effects or no association. Conclusions: Social media's role in health is nuanced, with predominant negative effects on behaviors and outcomes, underscoring the need for balanced policies, digital literacy programs, and longitudinal research to mitigate harms and amplify benefits.
